newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russian Duma urges bans on foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russian Duma urges bans on foreign investment.

text.p: Russia's lower house of parliament called on Friday for a wide-ranging ban on foreign investment in key sectors of the economy.

Deputies in the communist-dominated State Duma voted 261 to 10 in a first reading to ban foreign activity in some areas involving national security such as power supplies and telecoms, and limit it in others, such as oil and financial services.

Dozens of areas would be affected by the proposals, contained in amendments to the law on foreign investment, including production of relief maps, manufacturing non-military goods in military plants, advertising and precious metals.
"This law is just what is needed to stop the fragmentation of the country," senior Communist Party deputy Anatoly Lukyanov told the house during the debate.
The government already restricts foreign investment in sensitive areas such as oil, but the Duma's proposals would go much further.
Sergei Mikhailov, a senior Industry Ministry official, condemned the Duma move on foreign investment.
"I have to find money for enterprises, and there's none in the budget, so for that reason we have to look for private money," he told a news conference.
Traders on the Russian equities market, which has rallied more than 50 percent this year on a surge of foreign investment, said some investors were nervous but impact had been slight.
"I don't think people will take it seriously. It is obvious Russia needs foreign funds in these capital-intensive sectors," said Alexander Bubnovsky, head of sales at Alfa Capital.
The Communist Party says there is a danger foreigners will buy up Russian industry on the cheap.
Foreign direct investment in Russia totals only $6.6 billion, less than half the figure for Hungary, the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe said this week.
But foreign investors have started to pour money into Russian equities, arguing that in terms of the assets Russian companies control, the shares are extremely cheap.
The amended law says foreign investors should be treated in the same way as domestic entrepreneurs except in areas affecting national security.
Before the amendments can become law they would need to be passed in two further readings by the Duma and then approved by the Federation Council upper house and President Boris Yeltsin.
How existing investments would be affected remains unclear.
The amendments passed by the Duma say investors suffering a substantial deterioration in their business from changes in legislation would be able to appeal to a government body.
This in turn would have the option of allowing the foreign investor to continue operating for five years under conditions in which the original investment was made.
The proposed ban is contained in amendments to the law on foreign investment, which include two appendices listing areas where foreign investment should be forbidden or limited.

Areas in which foreign investment would be banned include: nuclear power; uranium mining; many types of military equipment; private security operations; production of banknotes and government securities; compulsory insurance; television and radio broadcasting; distribution and trade in electrical energy, and use of power lines; use of water reservoirs and canals; production of narcotics; production of globes and relief maps; air-traffic control and other forms of traffic control; real estate and land trade; production and distribution of ethyl spirit and alcohol products.

Areas in which foreign investment would be limited include: production of special energy equipment; oil; shipping and aviation; rail transport; building and operating airports and other traffic facilities; production of geological studies and geodesic equipment; production of certain medicines; mining and production of precious and rare metals and gems; purchase of goods containing precious metals; soil research; operations with securities and depositaries; genetic engineering; writing textbooks; operating specialised post-privatisation funds; space activity; transport and trade in radio-active materials; production of non-military goods at military plants; banking, insurance and other financial services; distribution of films and videos; wholesale and retail trade; printing; medical services; pensions; education; advertising; catering; road transport; hydro and thermal power stations; lotteries and casinos; employment services; commercial fish breeding; forestry; auditing and production of furs from wild animals.
